name: São Paulo
tagline: South America's biggest metropolis: skyscrapers, street art, world-class museums, immigrant neighbourhoods and one of the best restaurant scenes on the continent.
highlight: A mortadella sandwich in the Mercado Municipal, followed by an evening among the murals of Vila Madalena.
shortDescription: Brazil's financial and cultural capital: Avenida Paulista and MASP, Ibirapuera Park, the Municipal Market, Beco do Batman, Liberdade and a spectacular food and nightlife scene.
metaDescription: A São Paulo travel guide: Avenida Paulista, MASP, Ibirapuera Park, the Municipal Market, Beco do Batman, Liberdade, the Copan building, food, safety, where to stay and a three-day plan.

intro: São Paulo is the largest city in Brazil and in the southern hemisphere, with more than 12 million people in the city itself and over 20 million in the wider metropolitan area. It began as a Jesuit mission in 1554, grew rich on coffee in the 19th century and became the industrial and financial engine of Brazil in the 20th. Waves of immigrants from Italy, Japan, Lebanon, Germany, Spain and elsewhere, as well as migrants from the north-east of Brazil, have shaped its culture.

It is not a conventional beauty. The city is a concrete sea of towers, elevated highways and traffic, but it rewards those who look closer. Avenida Paulista, the main artery, has museums and cultural centres, Ibirapuera Park is a green oasis designed by Oscar Niemeyer, and neighbourhoods such as Vila Madalena and Liberdade have street art, bars and restaurants. Its food is among the best in Latin America.

São Paulo works well as a two- or three-day stop for people who like cities, food and culture. It is not a beach destination, and safety needs the usual big-city care, but its energy and diversity are unlike any other Brazilian city.

whyVisit.intro: São Paulo is the place to see modern, urban, multicultural Brazil, and to eat well.

points.title: A world-class food scene
points.text: From street food and Italian pizza to Japanese and Lebanese cooking, and top modern Brazilian restaurants.

points.title: Museums and art
points.text: MASP, the Pinacoteca, the Museum of the Portuguese Language and the Bienal.

points.title: Street art
points.text: Beco do Batman and the walls of Vila Madalena and the centre.

points.title: Immigrant neighbourhoods
points.text: Liberdade for Japanese and Asian culture, Bixiga for Italian, and Bom Retiro for Korean and Jewish heritage.

points.title: Nightlife and music
points.text: Clubs, live music and bars open every night.

attractionsIntro: Most sights are along or near Avenida Paulista and in the historic centre.

attractions.name: Avenida Paulista and MASP

image.alt: The Museu de Arte de São Paulo, MASP, a red modernist building raised on pillars

attractions.text: The city's main avenue, with skyscrapers, cultural centres and cafés. MASP, a modernist museum on red pillars by Lina Bo Bardi, has one of the best art collections in Latin America. The avenue is closed to cars on Sundays.
attractions.tip: Go on a Sunday for a street party.

attractions.name: Ibirapuera Park

image.alt: Trees and a pond in Ibirapuera Park in São Paulo

attractions.text: The city's central park, with lakes, trails and buildings designed by Oscar Niemeyer, including the Bienal pavilion and museums.
attractions.tip: A calm break from the city.

attractions.name: The Mercado Municipal

image.file: File:Municipal Market of São Paulo city.jpg
image.alt: The interior of the Mercado Municipal with stalls and stained glass

attractions.text: A grand 1933 market hall with stained glass, selling fruit, spices, cheese and cured meats, and famous for its mortadella sandwich and pastel de bacalhau.
attractions.tip: Go for a late breakfast or early lunch.

attractions.name: Beco do Batman

image.alt: Colourful murals and street art covering the walls of Beco do Batman

attractions.text: An alley in Vila Madalena covered in graffiti and murals, changing constantly, and surrounded by galleries and bars.
attractions.tip: Go in the afternoon, and stay for dinner.

attractions.name: Liberdade
attractions.text: The Japanese and Asian quarter, said to be home to the largest Japanese community outside Japan, with markets, temples and restaurants.
attractions.tip: Go on a Sunday for the street fair.

attractions.name: The Copan Building and Terraço Itália
attractions.text: Oscar Niemeyer's serpentine Copan apartment block, and the Terraço Itália rooftop, which give views across the city.

thingsToDoIntro: São Paulo rewards curiosity and appetite.

thingsToDo.title: Eat a mortadella sandwich
thingsToDo.text: A towering sandwich at the Mercado Municipal.

thingsToDo.title: Visit MASP
thingsToDo.text: See European masters and Brazilian art.
thingsToDo.tip: Free on Tuesdays, check the schedule.

thingsToDo.title: Join a street art tour
thingsToDo.text: Learn about the artists and history of the city's murals.

thingsToDo.title: Eat pizza
thingsToDo.text: The city has some of the best pizza outside Italy.

thingsToDo.title: Explore Liberdade
thingsToDo.text: Sushi, ramen, Japanese sweets and shops.

thingsToDo.title: Go out in Vila Madalena
thingsToDo.text: Bars, live music and restaurants, with a lively atmosphere.

foodIntro: São Paulo's food is the most diverse in Brazil, shaped by immigration.

foods.name: Mortadella sandwich
foods.text: A giant sandwich of thin-sliced mortadella at the Municipal Market.

foods.name: Pastel
foods.text: Crisp fried pastry filled with cheese, meat or cod, served with sugar-cane juice at street fairs.

foods.name: Pizza
foods.text: Thin, crisp pizzas in Italian-Brazilian tradition, in neighbourhoods such as Bixiga.

foods.name: Japanese food
foods.text: Sushi, sashimi and ramen, in the Liberdade and Aclimação neighbourhoods.

foods.name: Feijoada
foods.text: Black bean stew, served on Wednesdays and Saturdays.

foods.name: Coffee and pão de queijo
foods.text: Coffee from the state's plantations, and cheese bread.

accommodation.intro: Choose a base near Avenida Paulista or in Jardins and Vila Madalena.

areas.text: Hotels close to museums and restaurants.

areas.name: The centre
areas.text: Budget hotels, but avoid at night.

gettingThere.intro: São Paulo is Brazil's busiest air hub.

options.text: Direct flights from Europe, North America and other South American cities.
options.detail: Allow 1 to 1.5 hours to the centre, or take a train and metro.

options.text: About 1 hour to Congonhas or Guarulhos.

bestTime.headline: March–May and August–October
bestTime.summary: São Paulo has a mild, humid subtropical climate, with warm, rainy summers and cooler, drier winters.

seasons.text: Warm and rainy, with afternoon storms.
Cool and dry, with occasional cold snaps.

bestTime.avoid: January and February for heavy afternoon rain.

itinerary.title: Three days in São Paulo
itinerary.intro: The avenue and museums, markets and street art, and the parks.

days.title: Markets and art
days.afternoon: Beco do Batman and Vila Madalena.

tipsIntro: A few tips help you get the most out of the city.
tips: Use the metro, and use Uber or 99 at night.
Avoid the Cracolândia area and empty streets in the centre after dark.
Keep your phone out of sight, and carry only what you need.
Go to Avenida Paulista on Sunday.
Visit museums on weekdays, when they are less crowded.

faq.q: How many days do you need in São Paulo?
faq.a: Two or three days for museums, food and neighbourhoods.
Yes, for food and culture, if you like cities.
The main visitor areas are generally fine. Take the usual big-city precautions and avoid certain parts of the centre at night.
Rio for scenery and beaches, and São Paulo for food and culture. Many visitors do both.

faq.q: What is the best time to visit?
faq.a: March to May and August to October.
